A wildfire near Lahaina was reported at 6:40 am HST and was contained within 3 hours. Another fire was reported around 3:30pm and prompted evacuation orders by 4:30 pm. However, power lines downed by the damaging winds closed roads and restricted evacuation routes. Wildfire continued to spread rapidly and quickly became out of control. The Coast Guard rescued people entering the Pacific Ocean who were escaping the fire. They rescued seventeen people including two children and assisted forty survivors on shore. At around 11:52 pm the Hawaii National guard was deployed on Maui as wildfires continued to burn out of control.  At 1:20 AM on August 9, over 14,000 customers were without power, and at 5:03 AM, the fire damaged much of the historic banyan tree that was imported to Maui in 1873 from India. At 9:25 am on August 9, over 2,100 people were seeking refuge in Maui shelters, a number that would increase throughout the month, reaching a peak of 8,000 in September. At 12:45 pm on August 9, more than 14,000 people were transported off Maui with another 14,500 waiting to be moved. The fire burned 2,170 acres and destroyed most of the historic town of Lahaina, including over 2,200 structures burned mostly or completely to the ground. There were 102 confirmed fatalities and at least 32 injuries. The fire also destroyed about 4,000 cars, of which 1,000 had been abandoned on public roadways. As of late October, the Coast Guard had recovered and removed 86 vessels from Lahaina Small Boat Harbor, in addition to 9,400 gallons of petroleum products and 3,300 pounds of hazardous materials.

At approximately 800 pm HST, a mesoscale convective system was observed moving over the Kauai Channel towards Oahu. At around 900 pm HST, this mesoscale convective system moved over the west side of Oahu, then the Northern half of Oahu, and began to deliver large amounts of heavy rain. Due to the slow moving nature of this weather system, enormous rain amounts accumulated in a very short time frame. At approximately 1000 pm HST, stream levels rose above flood thresholds and reservoirs filled up. From 1100 pm HST to 200 AM HST, a massive flood wave surged through the North Shore. Multiple roads became impassable across Northern Oahu, Haleiwa became completely cut off, and multiple homes and many cars got swept away in flood waters. Many homes and cars that were not washed away were heavily damaged beyond use or habitation. Businesses were also flooded, and an ambulance was reportedly lost due to the rising flood waters. With the help of police officers, the crew escaped the ambulance through the side window. There were over 200 rescues by first responders and residents, these rescues included rescues from police, fire, national guard, and lifeguards. 10 people were taken to the ER with non critical hypothermia due to prolonged exposure to the flood waters. Much of the destruction and rescues were reported in Waialua and Haleiwa. However the damage spread to the northeast section of Oahu where multiple homes were inundated with flood waters.  Over 171 million dollars in damages were reported across Oahu's public schools from the Department of Education and officials put the total costs of the storm island wide above 1 billion dollars .

With deep water covering the roadway, Kamehameha V Highway became impassable near mile marker 8 on the island of Molokai.
Highway 11 was closed in the Kawa Flats area of the Kau District on the Big Island of Hawaii because of deep water on the roadway.

Flooding waters covered a portion of Kapaa Quarry Road and Kamehameha Hwy near Kahaluu in windward Oahu, as well as a portion of H-1 in downtown Honolulu. Flood waters also entered homes in Pearl City and Moiliili and an electrical substation in Iwilei. Landslides also blocked portions of Kamehameha Hwy near Kaaawa and Farrington Hwy near Makua Valley.

Winds, from various directions, gusted over 100 mph during a period that lasted more than one day over the summits of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa on the Big Island of Hawaii. Winds also gusted over 90 mph on the Haleakala Summit on Maui.

An estimated 6 to 10 inches of snow fell, after about 2 inches of rain that fell and froze, over the summits of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa on the Big Island of Hawaii.  Some snow drifts were 3 to 5 feet in depth.
Kuhio Highway was closed near the Hanalei Bridge due to flooding across the roadway in the northern section of Kauai.
Heavy rain flooded Kapaa Quarry Road on the windward side of Oahu.
Downpours caused the Hanalei River to overflow onto Kuhio Highway near the Hanalei Bridge in the northern part of Kauai.

Highway 190 on the Big Island was closed between the Saddle Road junction and Waimea due to flooding waters that overflowed from Kamakoa Gulch.  This was an impact from the Mana Road burn scar, the result of an earlier fire that devastated the local area.
